# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–39 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 16)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to **Chapter 39 (autumn, extending into Thursday morning after failed elopement, with village scenes from Yarlton, Dunholt, Dunwick, Salwick, Mirecombe, Miremere, Harrowgate).**
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool, Conservative club in the City, Mount Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Dunwick; Salford; Yarlton; coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Salwick, Salmere, Mirecombe, Miremere).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn). Feten Lindner followed her to Harrowgate within the month (likely died).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Overdrawing her account at bank. Chapter 39: Discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk at 6–7 A.M., fell in gutter. Suffering over his involvement with Marie Melmotte's elopement, money owed. Confessed troubles to Mr. Broune (Thursday evening in her sanctum). Received his counsel: must rid herself of Felix, extract money story, send word to him early next morning. Sent letter to Mr. Broune next morning with Felix's account: claims Melmotte owed him £600; received £250 from Marie via Didon; lost this money at play. Lady Carbury acknowledged in letter she cannot justify believing her son's account.

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Chapter 38–39 (ELOPEMENT PLAN FAILED)**: Received £250 from Didon Monday 4 P.M.; understood he must go to New York. Planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones," spend Tuesday with Ruby at Music Hall, depart Wednesday 5 P.M. for Liverpool. Attended Music Hall 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; Ruby did not appear; returned to club. Found Dolly Longestaffe and Miles Grendall; whispered to Grendall to convert I.O.U.s to cash; Grendall refused. Had been drinking freely; called Grendall to card-room with Dolly as witness; Grendall again refused. Played at Beargarden till 4 A.M.; intoxicated and almost penniless; made unpleasant remarks about Miles Grendall (accused of cheating at loo, appealing to Dolly as witness); Dolly said he knew nothing about it; desperate row ensued; Lord Grasslough opined more than one person might be turned out. **Between 6–7 A.M. Wednesday knocked at Welbeck Street door; latch-key inefficient; door locked. Lady Carbury opened door; he was sodden with gutter, drunk. Lied claiming "old shap stopped ush" (Melmotte); Melmotte was actually asleep in Grosvenor Square, ignorant of plot. Felix stumbled upstairs; mother removed his clothes and boots; he fell asleep. Chapter 39: Still in bed Thursday, 2–5 P.M., sick and ill and sore from head to foot; uneasy slumber only; found no comfort; feared attack by outer world. Remained in bed Friday morning awaiting refreshment.** Still in London as of Chapter 39 (Thursday).

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew; determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street; she told mother loves someone else and praises Roger as "rock of strength." **Chapter 39: Retired from sofa while mother attended Felix. Turned matter over in mind: Could it be right to marry one man when loves another? Roger worships the ground she trod; all mother said of him true—soft heart, sweet nature—but Hetta knows he is man of high honour and noble courage. In her condition he would be the very friend whose advice she could ask, had he not been the lover desirous of making her wife. Could sacrifice much for mother; could doom herself to poverty, loneliness, heart-rending regrets. But did not know how to give herself into arms of man she did not love.**

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement Attempt

**Marie Melmotte**: **Chapter 38 (ELOPEMENT EXECUTED BUT INTERCEPTED)**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon; discussed American clergyman marrying them on board. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes. Marie and Didon followed in second cab with smaller luggage. Reached Euston Square, obtained tickets in French, departed. ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM: Upon train arrival, gentleman addressed her: "You, I think, are Miss Melmotte." Didon became voluble in French, claiming young lady was Mademoiselle Racine. Gentleman insisted, used her English. Marie declared she spoke French; he countered "And English too." Gentleman told them to return to London; would accompany them. Didon asserted legality of position. Gentleman spoke low: cheque changed from father's house; father would pardon when she rejoined him; could arrest her on cheque if forced; would not let her board. If she traveled back, no unnecessary inconvenience. Gentleman telegraphed Grosvenor Square during journey. At Euston Square met by Melmotte carriage. Marie taken home; boxes to follow at interval.** **Chapter 39: Marie aware she would be interrogated. Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking, reminding her of generosity (carriages, horses, bracelets, brooches, silks, gloves). Marie shows determination: "I don't think that mamma cares. It's papa. I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." She continued: "I would. Why is a girl to be made to marry to please any one but herself? I won't. And it's very mean saying that I stole the money. I always take what I want, and papa never says anything about it." Melmotte angry at Sir Felix beyond measure; man pledged in writing to abstain from marrying Marie, renounced under signature his intention. Learned all details of cheque for £250—paid at bank to Didon, who gave it to Sir Felix. Marie acknowledged Sir Felix received money. Melmotte would prosecute baronet for stealing money if possible. After interrogation, Melmotte received £250 back from Mr. Broune on Sir Felix's behalf (via Broune as intermediary).** Melmotte has decided to write to Lord Nidderdale, making clear breast of matter; believes openness best supports chance of keeping young lord to his suit. Young lord has been aware of Felix difficulty weeks past, has not relaxed suit. Melmotte now urges Nidderdale to renew suit; emphasizes Marie has stronger will than previously thought, never gave Nidderdale encouragement since Christmas, but failed elopement will assist rather than impede Nidderdale's views.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Crisis, Correspondence, and Resolution (Chapter 39)**: Returned to London Monday morning from Suffolk. Sat in his lodgings thinking of his condition; almost wished he had taken Melmotte's offer and gone to Mexico. Dreamed of life like Roger Carbury's—seemed far beyond reach. **Twice lately gone to Islington determined to see Mrs. Hurtle for last time. Took her to Lowestoft, equally firm in resolution to end bonds. Now promised to go again to Islington; aware if he failed she would come to him. No end to it.** **Wrote to Mrs. Hurtle: acknowledged circumstances made their lives and temperaments too different for happy marriage; fault was his; better to own fault and take consequences than marry with consciousness marriage would be sorrow and repentance. Broke engagement before knowing this girl; did not break because came to love her. No grounds for hoping love will lead to results. Told her condition of mind exactly. If possible would compensate injury or undergo retribution; could she exact? Thought further meeting avail nothing. But if she wishes, will come last time.** **Mrs. Hurtle's Response**: Letter duly reached Paul. She suffered many injuries; this worst, most unpardonable, most unmanly. Called him coward, false liar. He bound himself by most solemn obligation joining man and woman together, then told her they go for nothing because do not suit his view. Has no brother, no man near her; or he would not dare. Called him coward. Talked of compensation; does he mean money? As to retribution: yes. He shall suffer. Desires him to come to her according to promise; will find her with horsewhip in hand. Will whip him till has not breath in body. Then will see what he dares do—whether will drag her into court for assault. Should he be afraid and break promise, she will come to him. Will make London too hot to hold him; if not find him will go with story to every friend he has.** **Paul started immediately for Islington upon receiving letter. Had no desire to delay meeting. Chapter 39 Meeting Details**: Paul shown into Mrs. Hurtle's room. His mind altogether intent on his own troubles. Mrs. Hurtle very calm but quietness assumed; could convert into violence at any moment; her eye foretold spring of wild-cat. She pointed seat at distance from herself. **Paul sat. Mrs. Hurtle spoke softly, then raised voice and half-lifted in seat: "Why should a gentleman trouble himself to say any more,--than that he has changed his mind?... But I should not. I at least will be true. I should take you, Paul,--still take you; with a confidence that I should yet win you to me by my devotion. I have still some kindness of feeling towards you,--none to that woman who is I suppose younger than I, and gentler, and a maid." Asked advice what to do next. Has given up every friend for him. Has no home; Mrs. Pipkin's room more her home than any other spot. Has all world to choose from but no reason for choice. Has property. What shall she do with it? If could die and be no more heard of, Paul should be welcome to it. Asked: "You are in some degree responsible,--are you not,--for my loneliness?"** **Paul suggested she better remain here; does good to Mrs. Pipkin. Mrs. Pipkin went into hysterics yesterday when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Mrs. Pipkin would starve in America; Mrs. Hurtle desolate here. Then paused, absolute silence for minute. Admitted had much more to say; that was third letter written. Handed him sheet containing threat of horsewhip. Then handed him scrap written at Lowestoft. She had thought of womanly weakness in soft moment; wrote other letter.** **She said: "Nay, I would not hurt you,--not at this moment. Why should I be such a victim? Why should life be an utter blank to me, while you have everything before you? There, you have seen them all. Which will you have?" Paul knelt. She said: "But it will be when you have left me. Why should you kneel there? You do not love me. A man should kneel to a woman for love, not for pardon." She put hand upon his forehead, pushed back his hair, looked into his face. Asked: "I wonder whether that other woman loves you. I do not want an answer, Paul. I suppose you had better go." Took his hand and pressed it to her breast. Asked: "Tell me one thing. When you spoke of--compensation, did you mean--money?"** **After Paul left, Mrs. Hurtle rang bell for Ruby and asked Mrs. Pipkin to come. Announced standing upright in middle of room with smile on face: "Everything is over between me and Mr. Montague." She has decided to depart from Islington.** Ruby opened door for Paul during meeting; asks "Is Sir Felix still in London?" Greets Paul with unhappy countenance; holds baby in arms; little child (Sally) hanging on to her dress.

## Augustus Melmotte and Imperial Reception Crisis (Chapter 39)

**Events**: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, altogether ignorant of elopement plot. Later interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her. Had got back his daughter, half inclined to let matter rest there; but all household aware she went to meet Sir Felix, received condolence of certain friends in city. By two o'clock matter known to everybody. Would hear of it, all trouble taken in Lord Nidderdale direction taken in vain. Stupid fool of a girl. His anger against Sir Felix infinitely more bitter than against his daughter. Man pledged in writing to abstain from marrying Marie; given signed pledge; renounced under signature his intention. Received £250 back from Mr. Broune (Felix's intermediary); crumpled cheque and put it into pocket. Clever enough to perceive any idea of prosecuting Sir Felix must be abandoned. Invited Lord Nidderdale to lunch at Conservative club in the City before Railway Board meeting. Urged Nidderdale to visit Grosvenor Square Sunday morning about noon to renew suit with Marie. Escaped back stairs with Nidderdale to avoid waiting people who think he should attend business from morning to night.

**Imperial Reception Confrontation (Chapter 39)**: Melmotte stood directly in way of Mr. Wilson, Secretary of State, and repeated demand: "I am desirous of being presented to his Imperial Majesty. Will you do me the honour of making my request known to Mr. Wilson?" Insisting: "It is generally understood, I believe, that the Emperor is to do me the honour of dining at my poor house on Monday. He don't dine there unless I'm made acquainted with him before he comes. I mean what I say. I ain't going to entertain even an Emperor unless I'm good enough to be presented to him. Perhaps you'd better let Mr. Wilson know, as a good many people intend to come." Lord Alfred whispered: "upon my word it isn't the thing. They're only Indian chaps and Eastern swells who are presented here,--not a fellow among 'em all who hasn't been in India or China, or isn't a Secretary of State, or something of that kind." Melmotte responded: "Then they should have done it at Windsor, or at the ball. By George, Alfred! I'm in earnest, and somebody had better look to it. If I'm not presented to his Imperial Majesty to-night, by G----, there shall be no dinner in Grosvenor Square on Monday. I'm master enough of my own house, I suppose, to be able to manage that." Threatened: "There shall be no dinner. I'll be d---- if any of the lot shall dine in Grosvenor Square on Monday." Under secretary Lord De Griffin intervened: "If you will be so kind as to follow me." Melmotte resolved upon making a little speech, forgetful at the moment of interpreters,--of the double interpreters whom the Majesty of China required; but the awful, quiescent solemnity of the celestial one quelled even him, and he shuffled by without saying a word even of his own banquet. **Had gained his point, and, as he was taken home to poor Mr. Longestaffe's house in Bruton Street, was intolerable. Lord Alfred tried to escape after putting Madame Melmotte and her daughter into the carriage, but Melmotte insisted on his presence.** **Continued ranting in carriage**: "D---- the election, sir. I stand before the electors of Westminster as a man of business, not as a courtier,--as a man who understands commercial enterprise, not as one of the Prince's toadies... I think myself quite as great a man as any Prince... I'll teach them a lesson before long... They tell me that Lord De Griffin has sixty thousand a-year to spend. What's sixty thousand a year? Didn't I make him go on my business? And didn't I make 'em do as I chose?... I know more of men and women than some of you fellows do, who think you know a great deal." This went on through whole of long cigar. Afterwards, Lord Alfred slowly paced his way back to his lodgings in Mount Street, thinking deeply whether there might not be means of escaping from his present servitude. Said to himself over and over again: "Beast! Brute! Pig!"

**Possessed only by belief that England's glory demanded his return for Westminster; thoroughly ignorant of political questions, political history, Parliament's working, nationality, or forms of government; had never read a book in his life; knew nothing of Hampden, Somers, or Pitt; never reflected how despotic monarch or federal republic might affect him; yet fully confident England demanded Melmotte for Westminster.**

**Imperial Dinner Preparations (Chapter 39)**: Servants and workmen gave Father Barham admittance to house in great confusion. Wreaths of flowers and green boughs being suspended, last daubs of heavy gilding given to wooden capitals of mock pilasters, incense being burned to kill smell of paint, tables being fixed and chairs moved; enormous set of open presses being nailed together for accommodation of hats and cloaks. Hall was chaos. Father Barham made his way to banqueting hall. **Melmotte stood in front of chair arranged for Emperor, with hat on one side of head, very angry indeed. Had been given to understand when dinner first planned that he was to sit opposite to august guest—by which he had conceived he was to have seat immediately in face of Emperor of Emperors, of the Brother of the Sun, of the Celestial One himself. Now explained to him that this could not be done. In face of the Emperor there must be wide space, so that his Majesty might be able to look down the hall; royal princesses who sat next to Emperor, and royal princes who sat next to princesses, must also be so indulged. In this way Mr. Melmotte's own seat became really quite obscure. Lord Alfred was having very bad time of it. "It's that fellow from 'The Herald' office did it, not me," he said, almost in a passion. "I don't know how people ought to sit. But that's the reason."**

**Melmotte's Charitable Maneuvering**: Presented hundred guineas towards erection of altar for new church of St. Fabricius, in Tothill Fields. Donation accompanied by letter from Mr. Melmotte's secretary, which left but little doubt that new member for Westminster would be member, and no inconsiderable member, of Catholic party in House during next session. Mr. Alf's newspaper bit at this, noting apparent hypocrisy with Protestant support. Melmotte and his manager not foolish enough to allow it to actuate them. He had thrown his bread upon the waters, assisting St. Fabricius with one hand and Protestant curates with other, must leave results to take care of themselves. If Protestants chose to believe he was hyper-protestant, and Catholics that he was tending towards papacy, so much the better for him. Any enthusiastic religionists wishing to enjoy such convictions would not allow themselves to be enlightened by manifestly interested malignity of Mr. Alf's newspaper.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her against Felix; extracted promise not to see him again; spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about late hours. Encountered Paul and Mrs. Hurtle at Lowestoft; greeted coldly; reproved Paul severely. Counselled marriage with her would be destruction. Upon Paul's return, expressed satisfaction: "Let her follow you, and bear it. Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence." **Chapter 39: Mr. Hepworth visited him one morning; they discussed attempted elopement. Roger said: "I know nothing about it, and I do not intend to ask. Of course I did know when they were down here that he hoped to marry her, and I did believe that she was willing to marry him. But whether the father had consented or not I never enquired." Hepworth opined Felix "A failure! Of course he's a failure, whether rich or poor;--a miserable imposition, a hollow vulgar fraud from beginning to end,--too insignificant for you and me to talk of, were it not that his position is a sign of the degeneracy of the age. What are we coming to when such as he is an honoured guest at our tables?"**

**Chapter 39 Philosophical Discussion with Bishop**: Roger discussed Melmotte's fitness for Parliament with unknown Bishop (suggests Father Barham or similar clergy). Roger argued: "Men reconcile themselves to swindling. Though they themselves mean to be honest, dishonesty of itself is no longer odious to them. Then there comes the jealousy that others should be growing rich with the approval of all the world,--and the natural aptitude to do what all the world approves. It seems to me that the existence of a Melmotte is not compatible with a wholesome state of things in general." Bishop countered: existence of Melmotte not necessarily pernicious if he would vote Conservative; country is changing. Bishop observed: "It is very hard to see into the minds of men, but we can see the results of their minds' work. I think that men on the whole do live better lives than they did a hundred years ago. There is a wider spirit of justice abroad, more of mercy from one to another, a more lively charity, and if less of religious enthusiasm, less also of superstition." Argued improvement proceeds from society as whole, not small things beneath eyes. Roger referenced Roman tribune from Horace's ode, suggesting Melmotte parallels corrupt ancients. Bishop countered: "Your friend in the ode probably had a bad time of it, in spite of his farms and his horses. The world perhaps is managed more justly than you think, Mr. Carbury."

**Father Barham at Carbury Manor**: Roof blown off Father Barham's cottage by wind; Roger Carbury, though affection for priest waning, offered him shelter while damage being repaired. Shelter at Carbury Manor much more comfortable than priest's own establishment, even with roof on; Father Barham in clover. Reading "The Surplice" when Roger entered library.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway
**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury (attempted to flee), Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague. **Board meeting Chapter 39: Sir Felix did not attend; nor did Paul Montague. Lord Nidderdale had declined. Mr. Longestaffe banished by hunger. Chairman supported only by Lord Alfred and Mr. Cohenlupe; work got through well. After Board, Melmotte and Cohenlupe retired together.**

## Minor Characters and Village Scenes
Didon (Marie's attendant, executed elopement plan). Miles Grendall (Secretary to Melmotte; does not pay debts of honour; at club Monday evening; refused Felix's petition twice; present at Melmotte's office Chapter 39). Robert (Marie's servant; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes). Lord Nidderdale (young lord; long-standing suitor for Marie despite Felix difficulty; noted Felix's portmanteaux at club Monday night; remarked "By George! Fancy taking a girl to New York! It was plucky." Melmotte urged him to visit Sunday noon to renew suit; Nidderdale thought of position and said perhaps would come; declined lunch and Board meeting; had strong opinion Board was "rot"; stated Marie never gave him slightest encouragement since Christmas). Dolly Longestaffe (at club Monday evening; when Felix accused Grendall of cheating at loo, appealed to Dolly as witness; Dolly said he knew nothing about it; banished by hunger from Board meeting). Lord Alfred Grendall (absolutely dependent on Melmotte; born and bred gentleman; found position under Melmotte almost insupportable; afflicted spending hours with Melmotte in borough, standing close to him at meetings; when Mr. Beauclerk (cousin, wealthy builder, Conservative politician) suggested he speak to Melmotte about manner, Lord Alfred could not restrain himself; observed by Lord Nidderdale to have invested part of recent savings in cutting whip; paced back to Mount Street thinking of escape from servitude; nudged heavily in ribs by Marquis of Auld Reekie at reception). Sir Merton Longestaffe (determined no London expenses; desires to sell Pickering; Dolly refused consent unless half produce given to him). Adolphus Longestaffe (£5,000 pay tradesmen, £20,000 free property; threatened Squercum; Melmotte's house Bruton Street). Georgiana Longestaffe (made protest; received invitation to stay with Melmottes; present Grosvenor Square Sunday). Mr. Wilson (Secretary of State). Lord De Griffin (under secretary; intervened at reception). Lionel Lupton (young aristocrat, MP; inoculated with idea that Melmotte's interests in Parliament essential).

**Village characters and backdrop (Chapter 39)**: Jozek Hollett, Eldette, Aewyn, Cobin Corrett, Wewyn Corrett, Colan Lindson, Daena Wexwood, Zanar Hollwood. Daena and Zanar wed at Miremere with half parish looking on; couple lived there from then on. Ridette could keep it no longer and told wife of Daric Brackwood that harbour master of Harrowgate takes bribes. Lubin fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Rain threatening since morning but held off. Wind came off water with smell of salt and tar. Gulls quarreled over heap of fish heads by steps. Light went early. Dog barked at nothing then went quiet.
